You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

{"title":"Soy vs Beeswax Candles (Plus Coconut-Soy): Which Candle Wax Is Right for You?","meta_description":"Soy vs beeswax candles, plus coconut-soy: how each wax differs in scent, format, burn time and care, and how to pick the right candle for your home.","slug":"soy-vs-beeswax-candles-coconut-soy-guide","markdown":"If you're weighing soy vs beeswax candles, here's the short answer. Soy is a lovely pick for scented jar candles. Beeswax shines as unscented tapers for the dinner table. Coconut-soy blends sit in between as a creamy, scented container option. The right wax comes down to how you like to use candles at home: for fragrance, for cozy ambiance, or for a warm glow over a meal.

## Soy vs beeswax at a glance

All three waxes have their fans, and each one tends to show up in a different kind of candle. Here's a quick, friendly overview:

- **Soy wax** is a plant-based wax made from soybean oil. It's widely used for scented container candles because it's soft and works nicely in jars. Our Sea Salt Soy Candle is made of 100% soy wax [F2].
- **Coconut-soy blends** mix coconut wax with soy for a creamy, smooth wax that's popular in container candles. Our Cedar Wood-Wick Candle is made with a coconut and soy wax blend [F13].
- **Beeswax** is a natural wax produced by honeybees. It's firm enough to hold its shape, which is why it's a classic choice for tapers. Our Beeswax Taper Candles are made of pure beeswax from Maine apiaries [F22].

So before you pick a wax, ask yourself what you want the candle to do. Do you want your living room to smell amazing? Do you want a crackling, cabin-like mood? Or do you want a simple, unscented flame on the table? Each wax has a sweet spot, and we'll walk through them one by one.

## Soy candles: an easygoing choice for scented jars

Soy wax has become a go-to for scented candles, and it's easy to see why. It's a soft, plant-based wax with a relatively low melting point, so it settles comfortably into a jar and melts into a pool that releases fragrance as it warms. Because it lives in a container, a soy candle is also an easy, low-fuss option: no candlestick needed, just a flat, heat-safe surface.

[Our Sea Salt Soy Candle](P1) is made of 100% soy wax and poured by hand in Portland, Maine [F2, F3]. It's made by Tidewell, right here in our own range [F10]. The candle has a cotton wick that's lead-free, which matters if you pay attention to what's burning in your home [F4, F5]. Its scent notes are sea salt, driftwood and sage, for a fresh, coastal feel [F9].

It comes in an 8 oz amber glass jar topped with a tin lid, handy for keeping dust off between burns [F1, F7, F8]. You can expect a burn time of about 45 hours [F6].

{{P1}}

## Coconut-soy blends: soy with a twist

If you like soy but want a slightly different feel, a coconut-soy blend is worth a look. Coconut wax is often combined with soy to create a creamy, smooth wax that sits beautifully in a container. Think of it as a close cousin of straight soy: still a scented container candle, just with a blended base.

[Our Cedar Wood-Wick Candle](P2) is made with a coconut and soy wax blend [F13]. The real personality here is the wick: it has a cherry-wood wick that crackles as it burns, so you get a soft, fireside sound along with the glow [F14]. Its scent notes are cedar, black pepper and vetiver, a warm and woodsy combination [F19].

This candle is 12 oz and comes in a 12 oz ceramic vessel [F11, F16]. That vessel is reusable, so it can live on as a planter, a pen pot or a little catch-all [F17]. It has a burn time of about 60 hours [F15].

{{P2}}

## Beeswax candles: natural, unscented and made for the table

Beeswax has been used for candles for a very long time. It's made by honeybees, has a naturally golden color, and carries a faint, natural honeyed aroma of its own. That's one reason beeswax is so often left unscented: it doesn't need added fragrance to feel special. It's also firm, so it holds a tall, slim shape well, which makes it a natural fit for tapers in candlesticks.

Unscented candles are especially nice at the dinner table, where you want the food to be the star rather than a strong fragrance. A pair of beeswax tapers adds warmth without competing with anything on your plate.

[Our Beeswax Taper Candles](P3) are made of pure beeswax from Maine apiaries and are unscented [F22, F23]. They come as a pair, with two tapers that are 10 inches long [F20, F21]. Each one has a standard 7/8-inch base that fits most candlesticks, so they should slip right into holders you already own [F24]. Each taper burns about 8 hours [F25]. They're also dripless when kept away from drafts, which means less wax on your tablecloth [F26].

{{P3}}

## Burn time and care tips for each wax

Here's how the stated burn times compare across our three candles. Keep in mind that a jar candle and a taper are quite different formats, so this is more about knowing what to expect than picking a winner.

| Candle | Wax | Wick and format | Stated burn time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sea Salt Soy Candle | 100% soy [F2] | Lead-free cotton wick in an amber glass jar [F4, F5, F7] | About 45 hours [F6] |
| Cedar Wood-Wick Candle | Coconut and soy blend [F13] | Crackling cherry-wood wick in a ceramic vessel [F14, F16] | About 60 hours [F15] |
| Beeswax Taper Candles | Pure beeswax [F22] | Pair of 10-inch tapers [F20, F21] | About 8 hours each [F25] |

### General candle care

A few simple habits help any candle burn more evenly and look better for longer:

- **Keep candles out of drafts.** Open windows, fans and air vents can make a flame flicker, burn unevenly and leave soot.
- **Trim cotton wicks before relighting.** A common rule of thumb is to trim a cotton wick to about 1/4 inch before each burn [G].
- **Give the first burn time.** On a container candle's first light, let the melted wax reach the edges of the jar to help avoid tunneling.
- **Don't overdo a single session.** General guidance is to burn a container candle for no more than four hours at a time [G].
- **Never leave a flame unattended,** and always set candles on a stable, heat-safe surface.

### Wax-specific tips

- **Wood wicks:** The cherry-wood wick on the Cedar Wood-Wick Candle should be trimmed to 3 mm before each burn [F18].
- **Beeswax tapers:** Keep the Beeswax Taper Candles away from drafts so they stay dripless [F26]. Their 7/8-inch base fits most candlesticks, so make sure each taper sits upright and snug in its holder [F24].

## So which wax should you choose?

There's no single best candle wax, just the one that matches your moment. Here's a simple guide:

- **Choose soy for a classic scented jar candle.** If you want fragrance filling the room, the Sea Salt Soy Candle brings notes of sea salt, driftwood and sage [F9].
- **Choose coconut-soy with a wood wick for crackling, cozy atmosphere.** The Cedar Wood-Wick Candle has a cherry-wood wick that crackles as it burns, and its stated burn time of about 60 hours is longer than the soy candle's roughly 45 hours [F6, F14, F15].
- **Choose beeswax tapers for an unscented dinner-table glow.** The Beeswax Taper Candles are unscented and have a standard base that fits most candlesticks [F23, F24].

Of course, plenty of homes have room for all three: a scented jar in the living room, a crackling wood wick for chilly evenings, and a pair of tapers ready for dinner with friends. Browse our full [Candles collection](L1) to find the wax and format that suit the way you like to light up your home."}
